pumac-2024-combinatorics-a-07.title: Split 20 as 4 times 5
pumac-2024-combinatorics-a-07.body:
By the Chinese remainder theorem, write each exponent $k\in\mathbb Z_{20}$ as $(a,b)\in\mathbb Z_4\times\mathbb Z_5$, so $\omega^k=i^a\zeta^b$ with $\zeta=e^{2\pi i/5}$. For a subset $T$, let $B_a=\{b:(a,b)\in T\}\subseteq\mathbb Z_5$ and $P_a=\sum_{b\in B_a}\zeta^b$. Then
$$\sum_{T}\omega^k=(P_0-P_2)+i\,(P_1-P_3).$$
The numbers $P_a$ lie in $\mathbb Q(\zeta)$, which has degree $4$ and does not contain $i$ (because $\mathbb Q(\zeta,i)=\mathbb Q(\zeta_{20})$ has degree $8$). So $1,i$ are linearly independent over $\mathbb Q(\zeta)$, and the sum is $0$ iff $P_0=P_2$ and $P_1=P_3$.

When is $\sum_{b\in B}\zeta^b=\sum_{b\in B'}\zeta^b$ for $B,B'\subseteq\mathbb Z_5$? The only rational relation among $1,\zeta,\dots,\zeta^4$ is that their sum is $0$, so $\mathbf 1_B-\mathbf 1_{B'}$ must be a multiple of the all-ones vector: either $B=B'$ ($32$ pairs), or $\{B,B'\}=\{\emptyset,\mathbb Z_5\}$ ($2$ ordered pairs). That is $34$ ordered pairs $(B,B')$.

So there are $34$ choices for $(B_0,B_2)$ and $34$ for $(B_1,B_3)$: $34^2=1156$ subsets.

**Answer: 1156**

pumac-2024-combinatorics-a-07.title: Computer check
pumac-2024-combinatorics-a-07.body:
Enumerating all $2^{20}$ subsets and testing whether the sum vanishes (numerically) finds $1156$ zero-sum subsets, as above.

**Answer: 1156**
